explanations.answer: The nations the LORD drove out
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Manasseh, Hezekiah's son and king of Judah, did evil by following the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. Copying a neighbor's cookie recipe is one thing. Copying the ways of nations God had already cleared out is something else entirely.

explanations.answer: The kings who ruled in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Close to a neighbor, but not the one on this page. Verse 2 says Manasseh followed the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. No Egyptian kings show up in that verse. Keep your eyes on those driven-out nations, friend.

Assyria isn't named in this verse, baker. The text says Manasseh followed the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. So the answer sits right there in verse 2, with no passport needed.

I know why you'd hope so, friend, because Hezekiah did the hard work of tearing them down. But verse 3 says Manasseh rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed. Somebody swept the whole floor and then the son dumped it all back out.

That's right, baker. Verse 3 says Manasseh rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed. All that tearing down, and the son put it right back up. It's like watching somebody un-bake a whole batch.
Altars it is, baker. Verse 3 says Manasseh raised up altars for Baal, a false god. He didn't just let the old places stand there. He built new ones and put the name of a false god on them.
Towers sound big and dramatic, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The text says Manasseh raised up altars for Baal. Altars were what he was after, not skyscrapers.
Palaces would be a fancy way to honor a false god, but that's not what verse 3 says. It says Manasseh raised up altars for Baal. No marble, no throne room, just altars.

Both, baker. Verse 5 says that in both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven. He didn't stop at one corner and call it a day. He covered the whole place, and I think that's why the verse is so heavy.

Not quite, friend. The verse says that in both courtyards of the house of the LORD, Manasseh built altars to all the host of heaven. That's a bigger job than one courtyard. He kept going until both had them.
Almost like he'd have stopped there, but the text says more. Verse 5 says he built altars to all the host of heaven in both courtyards of the house of the LORD. Not just one, baker. Both.

Mediums, baker. Verse 6 says Manasseh practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He went to people who claimed to reach the spirit world, and the text calls it great evil in the sight of the LORD. Papa will stick to asking the LORD, and a good oven timer.

Prophets would have been a turn in the right direction, friend. But verse 6 says Manasseh consulted mediums and spiritists. The prophets show up later in this passage, and they're the ones the LORD speaks through (2 Kings 21:10).
Priests don't make the list in this verse, baker. The text says Manasseh practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. That's the company he chose.

explanations.answer: They had to do all He commanded
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them…” and then names the whole Law that His servant Moses, Israel's leader, commanded them (2 Kings 21:8). The promise came with a condition. I'd never try a recipe and skip half the steps either.

explanations.answer: They had to defeat their enemies
explanations.explanation: That's not the condition in verse 8, friend. God said, “…if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them…” and then pointed to the whole Law that Moses, Israel's leader, commanded them. The condition was about listening and obeying. Winning battles isn't in that line.

explanations.answer: They had to build Him more altars
explanations.explanation: Papa has to say no to this one, baker. In verse 8 the LORD says, “…if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them…” and points to the Law that Moses, Israel's leader, commanded. Building altars isn't the condition. Doing what He commanded is.

True, baker. Verse 9 says the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray. The king was out front and the people followed. When a leader heads off the road, a lot of folks end up in the ditch with him.
The text says otherwise, friend. Verse 9 says the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray. So he didn't just go on his own. He took the people along with him.

Right, baker. Verse 9 says Manasseh led the people astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. Greater than the very nations God had destroyed. That's a hard line to read.
It goes the other way, friend. Verse 9 says the people did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. So it wasn't less. It was more.
Same would be bad enough, baker, but the text goes further. Verse 9 says the people did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. Greater, not equal.

I get why you'd hope for that, friend, but it's the opposite. In verse 12 the LORD, the God of Israel, says, “Behold, I am bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah…” Calamity, not peace and security. It's a hard word, and the LORD says it plainly.

That's right, baker. The LORD says He is bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah that the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it (2 Kings 21:12). No peace and security in that message. It's calamity.

A bowl, baker. In verse 13 God says He will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl, wiping it and turning it upside down. I know that picture from my own mixing bowls, wiped clean to the last crumb and flipped over on the rack. It's a heavy picture, and God says it plainly.

A table gets wiped all the time, friend, but that's not the picture here. Verse 13 says God will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl, wiping it and turning it upside down. The turning upside down is the part that goes with a bowl.

Floors get wiped too, baker, but verse 13 uses a different picture. God says He will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl, wiping it and turning it upside down. You don't turn a floor upside down.

Yes, baker. Verse 14 says God will forsake the remnant of His inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. It's a hard thing to read. Papa won't dress it up, because the text doesn't.

That would be a softer ending, friend, but it isn't the one in the text. Verse 14 says God will forsake the remnant of His inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. Delivered into those hands, not hidden from them.

No new land in this verse, baker. The LORD says He will forsake the remnant of His inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies (2 Kings 21:14). That's the message here, and it's a heavy one.

Egypt, baker. Verse 15 says they have done evil in God's sight and provoked Him to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day. That's a long stretch of time. The LORD is counting from the very beginning of their journey out.
Babylon isn't named in verse 15, friend. The LORD says they have provoked Him to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day. The starting point is Egypt.
Not Assyria, baker. In verse 15 the LORD says they have provoked Him to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day. Egypt is where that count begins.

That's right, baker. Verse 18 says Manasseh rested with his fathers and was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon reigned in his place. The text doesn't say more about the garden, so Papa won't either.
A fair guess, friend, but verse 18 says something different. Manasseh was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. The City of David doesn't come up in this verse.
Not the temple courtyard, baker. Verse 18 says Manasseh was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. That's where the text puts him, so that's where Papa leaves him.

True, baker. Verse 20 says Amon, Manasseh's son, did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. The son picked up right where his father left off. Papa wishes it were different, friend.
The text says the opposite, friend. Verse 20 says Amon, Manasseh's son, did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. So the apple didn't fall far from the tree here.

Idols, baker. Verse 21 says Amon walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. He didn't start his own thing. He kept on with what his father had handed him.
Rulers don't fit this verse, friend. It says Amon walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. The thing being worshiped is idols.
No serpents in verse 21, baker. The text says Amon walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. Idols are the word you want.
Yes, baker. Verse 23 says the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. It came from inside his own house. The text doesn't give a reason, so Papa won't make one up.
No brothers are named in this passage, friend. Verse 23 says the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. The plot came from his servants.
Babylon's king isn't in this scene, baker. Verse 23 says the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. The plot came from his own servants, right there in his home.

That's it, baker. Verse 24 says the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place. Josiah is Amon's son. One more name to keep close, friend.
Ahaz isn't the name in this verse, friend. Verse 24 says the people of the land made Amon's son Josiah king in his place. Josiah is the name to remember here.
Jehu isn't named in verse 24, baker. The text says the people of the land made Amon's son Josiah king in his place. Josiah is the one who takes the throne.
